newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - Hong Kong newspaper headlines - Apr 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Hong Kong newspaper headlines - Apr 21.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- MING PAO -- More than 1,000 people took part in a march organised by human rights groups to protest against consultative documents released by Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa's office earlier this month which suggested restrictions be placed on the freedoms of Hong Kong people.
-- APPLE DAILY -- Governor Chris Patten said China changed the voting arrangements for post-handover Hong Kong to reduce the number of pro-democracy candidates who could be elected.
-- WEN WEI PO -- An advance party of Chinese People's Liberation Army troops, made up of technical and coordination staff, were due to cross the border into Hong Kong on Monday.

-- China and Russia were negotiating a series of cooperation projects, including setting up a nuclear power plant and a gas pipeline and building a large Chinese shopping mall in Moscow. A disarmament agreement would also be signed by China, Russia and three other countries during the visit of Chinese President Jiang Zemin to Moscow this week.

-- ECONOMIC JOURNAL -- The mayor of Beijing, Zhang Baifa, said a Chinese property company would co-invest four billion yuan with New World Development to build an International Trade Centre in Beijing which would resemble Hong Kong's Convention and Exhibition Centre.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Hong Kong's four leading financial bodies -- the Securities and Futures Commission, the stock exchange, the futures exchange and the monetary authority -- confirmed they were seeking to unify the trading and regulatory organisations under one roof for the first time in Hong Kong's history.
-- China Resources Holdings was to purchase a 24.3 percent stake in Cosmo Machinery Enterprise and inject its interest in machinery maker Welltech into CME.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Government academics proposed that China include off-budget revenue -- or revenue excluded from the state spending plan -- to try to cut its budget deficit. Such a change in China's bookkeeping system could enable Beijing to meet its target of balancing the budget by 2000, they said.
